analysis.headline: Still quiet on the eve of Thanksgiving: no fresh bio×AI deal since this morning, but Capable's $38M seed for an in-house AI peptide lab (an October round held back this morning) is now confirmed and added
analysis.summary: Disclosed, closed bio×AI venture in the 45-day window is about $6.02B, with Isomorphic's $5B Series C (Nov 17) roughly 83% of it; Capable's $38M seed (Oct 16) is the only addition tonight. The 7-day closed-venture figure stays at about $126M (Boltz $110M, Leash $11M, Tesorai $5.3M), with MegaRobo's nearly $200M and the Chinese RMB rounds not counted in dollars. Last week's priced partnerships remain AstraZeneca–Tempus ($200M in fees over 2027–2031) and Vertex–Genomics (up to more than $220M plus royalties); the window's largest partnership headlines are Third Rock–Funnel (up to ~$2.16B) and argenx–Unnatural Products ($550M cash).

themes.title: AI labs move from vendor to drug owner, and design platforms find new kinds of buyers
themes.detail: Anthropic's S-1 sells drug discovery and lab-running models to public investors; after a $70 to $78 range and a book Bloomberg put at about six times covered, it confirmed on Nov 18 a price of $83 a share, raising $81.3B on 980M shares, the largest IPO on record, with Nasdaq trading from Nov 19; the company owns Mithril's muscular-dystrophy antibodies with candidates planned for 2027, and its drug R&D head now puts its pipeline at two to five preclinical programs. OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio and backs Chai and Biossil, the $1B drug-repurposing startup whose $153M round its fund led and which signed its first asset buy on Nov 2; Anthropic's Anthology Fund joined Basecamp's $140M. Generate Biomedicines' Q3 report (Nov 12) confirms a research collaboration with Anthropic on agentic CAR-T design, in which Claude helped shrink a key CAR component by about 70%. Former OpenAI staff founded Warp ($215M) and another is reportedly raising about $200M. Startups are getting the same pipeline-wide access: Pfizer is putting Edison Scientific's Kosmos agent to work on its internal data across oncology, immunology and internal medicine. Alphabet's Isomorphic closed a $5B Series C on Nov 17, co-led by Greenoaks and Sequoia with a16z new to the cap table, to take its first oncology and immunology programs toward the clinic and add biologics; it no longer gives a trial date. Two days later, on Nov 19, Merck became its fourth big-pharma partner after Lilly, Novartis and J&J, hiring IsoDDE for one oncology small-molecule target on Merck's own data, with an upfront, milestones and royalties, none quantified, and an option for Isomorphic to co-fund development for higher royalties. Buyers of AI design are widening beyond pharma: Third Rock Ventures, a company-creation venture firm, signed up to about $2.16B with Beijing's Funnel Biosciences for de novo antibodies against targets it chooses, its second such pact with a Chinese AI shop after Perpetual Medicine. At the small end, platforms are changing hands for stock: on Nov 10 Rakovina licensed Artemis.AI for its DNA-repair cancer targets for C$1M in shares and no cash, after iSpecimen's mostly-stock FoldLab purchase the week before. Chinese pharma is buying the same way at home: on Nov 13 Hansoh signed Hong Kong spin-off AilsynBio to find oral cyclic peptides against targets Hansoh picks, for up to RMB317M in total payments plus royalties, with Hansoh keeping the IP; and in a filing dated Nov 13, Luoxin Pharmaceuticals signed a non-binding cooperation with Insilico for digestive and metabolic drugs, with terms still to be negotiated. Software licences are growing inside pharma once they show results: on Nov 17 argenx extended Cradle's platform to more scientists and antibody programs after a first phase of lead optimisation, eight days after agreeing to buy Unnatural Products. Stock is also becoming the currency for consolidation one rung up: on Nov 17 Astromech, the Church and Lamm evolutionary-AI company valued at a reported $3.8B in August, agreed to buy sister Colossal spinout Form Bio for $230M in shares, adding AI design tools for gene-therapy constructs used by Lilly, Taysha and Solid Biosciences. Flagship is consolidating too, with no stock price attached: on Nov 11 it merged Valo Health with Montai Therapeutics under the Valo name, its second AI-platform merger in two weeks after Etcelera, leading with Montai's Phase 1 oral NRF2 agonist for ulcerative colitis. Japanese pharma keeps adding small Asian AI partners: on Nov 19 Astellas signed Korea's Bionsight, which pairs AI design with proteome-wide chemoproteomics, for a first-in-class innate-immune autoimmune program, terms undisclosed.

themes.title: AI moves into trial design, recruitment and clinical assets
themes.detail: In one week Boehringer and Microsoft agreed to test digital patient twins, AstraZeneca and Oracle signed a term sheet for AI trial recruitment, Atlas Bio raised a $10M seed to simulate Phase II trials, adsilico raised £10M to test medical devices on AI-built virtual patients, and BMS is using Claude to judge trial plans. Formation Bio went further, raising $600M to buy Phase 1–2 drugs and run them through its AI-native development platform, and Pathos's $237M also funds AI-led trials. Upstream of the clinic, AstraZeneca is also testing Tremont AI's toxicology-pathology models to speed preclinical safety reads. Biossil is running the same buy-don't-discover play at a smaller scale, picking up Theriva's paused Phase 1b/2a transplant-gut enzyme for $350K upfront and up to ~$91M in milestones. The services layer is drawing its own seed money too: on Nov 10 Proximal Ventures closed a $27.5M debut fund, backed by SignalFire and Kleiner Perkins, for startups automating the development work pharma outsources. Digital twins are reaching obesity too: on Nov 12 Unlearn said it is modelling untreated outcomes for Structure Therapeutics' oral GLP-1 extension study, with results at ObesityWeek (Nov 14–17). On Nov 12 Paris-based Orakl Oncology raised a $34M Series A, co-led by Norrsken VC and Singular with Bpifrance's patient fund joining, to forecast cancer-trial outcomes from patient tumour organoids plus clinical records, with four Sanofi assets as its first live test; a day earlier Switchpoint Bio raised a $5.3M pre-seed for AI-read blood methylation tests that track treatment response. Patient selection is becoming a deal of its own: on Nov 12 Prolong agreed to fund a Phase 2a of its oxygen-carrying drug PP-007 in ME/CFS, enrolling only patients whom ChronicleBio's multi-omic models place in an impaired-oxygen-delivery subtype; it is the first pharma deal for the startup led by former OpenAI executive Fidji Simo. The buy-and-develop model now has a Chinese seed-stage copy: on Nov 16 Qiming put RMB 40M into Shanghai's CataX AI, which will license early assets and take them to proof of concept with one clinical lead directing AI agents. Pharma is also buying real-world data for development: on Nov 18 Novo Nordisk paired its trial data with nference's federated health-record network to study cardiometabolic disease and design precision trials, with a side framework to start AI-native companies, terms undisclosed.

themes.title: Make, test and manufacture: money for the physical layer
themes.detail: Warp ($215M, chemistry robots), Multiply Labs ($75M, robotic biomanufacturing), Opentrons ($40M Series E for AI-driven benchtop robots already in most top-20 pharma labs), Xaira's X-Automate and Rivercell (€22M) all bet the bottleneck has moved from design to the lab. Danaher is building NVIDIA AI into its instruments for closed-loop experiments, and Anthropic's filing talks about models running lab robots. UCB's Nov 4 deal with Cradle and Roche's Nov 5 deal with Chai are the software side of the same split: pharma keeps the wet lab and licenses the design models (Cradle's retrain on each batch of UCB results; Chai-3 goes across Roche's discovery programs). The Nov 9 argenx deal puts a price on a working make-and-test loop: $550M in cash for machine learning tied to massively parallel peptide synthesis and direct-to-biology screening, bought by a partner that had watched it run for more than two years. XtalPi's Pierre Fabre deal the same day also sells AI and robotics as one package. Automation is also reaching the cell supply itself: on Nov 10 Mitsui Chemicals took a stake in iORGANBIO, which makes human cells and organoids for drug testing in a closed loop of AI, single-cell readouts and robots, and will co-develop culture conditions with it. Revenue-stage protein design is following the same playbook: Biomatter's $18M Series A (Nov 12), led by Astanor, pays for a 2,000 m² Vilnius design-and-test site to shorten enzyme design cycles for customers that include AstraZeneca and Sanofi. Chinese platforms are bundling the same way: BioMap's Nov 12 partner slate, with no terms, includes MegaStream TechBio, an automated closed-loop discovery venture with Harbour BioMed, and an AI biomanufacturing lab with Revvity. Oral macrocycles are the clearest product bet in this layer: argenx paid cash for Unnatural Products' peptide make-and-test loop on Nov 9, and four days later Hansoh hired AilsynBio's AI platform for the same drug class. The same bundle is drawing robot makers onto cap tables in China: Tourson Intelligence, which pairs an agent-driven protein design platform with its own wet lab, disclosed back-to-back Pre-A rounds (Nov 9, several hundred million yuan) with lab-automation maker MegaRobo among the backers. And the layer is now drawing sovereign money at scale: on Nov 19 MegaRobo, the same Beijing automation maker that backed Tourson, raised nearly $200M led by the Oman Investment Authority for robotic drug-screening labs (plus chip-line inspection), with a Hong Kong IPO filing still pending. Seed money is following the same logic: Capable's $38M seed (Oct 16), backed by Cathay Innovation and Abstract with Andrej Karpathy and Fidji Simo as angels, pays for a San Francisco lab that grew roughly elevenfold in weeks so AI-designed peptides can be made and tested fast enough to feed the next design, starting with a sleep program now entering preclinical safety work.

themes.title: Scale of data over number of platforms: big tech and pharma pay for the data layer, and investors now fund simulated data and physics too
themes.detail: Google DeepMind, Isomorphic and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open virtual-cell data coalition alongside DOE and NIH, and days later GSK, Pfizer and Sanofi became founding partners in Parse and Nomic's Cascade, a licensed 100M-cell immune perturbation dataset with matched protein readouts. Flagship merged three single-platform companies into Etcelera around a 150M-cell foundation model, BioGeometry raised past $100M to pair its design model with a virtual cell model and an automated lab, and ALLOX, Rivercell and now Venomics AI ($2.7M pre-seed for a venom-molecule atlas) raised early rounds to generate their own experimental data. Buyers now pay for data at scale, split into an open track (Biohub) and a closed, pharma-shared track (Cascade), which squeezes startups selling a proprietary atlas on its own. A third track appeared on Nov 5: Potential Sciences raised an eight-figure seed, co-led by the UK's Sovereign AI fund, to train chemistry models on physics-based quantum calculations run on GPUs instead of lab data. Fathom Therapeutics, which simulates protein motion with physics plus AI and counts Lilly Ventures among its backers, added Greek-American fund Kos to a Series A now put at $55M on Nov 6, a second physics-first chemistry bet in two days. Data holders outside pharma are starting to trade data for a share of the drugs rather than a fee: on Nov 9 Korean genomics firm 3billion put the genomes from its rare-disease testing business behind DeepLife's TwinCell virtual-cell model to co-develop small molecules against genetic modifier targets. Open-model companies are buying measured data too: on Nov 11 Boltz said it now trains the ADMET models in its BoltzMol-1 product on Excelra's curated GOSTAR solubility, lipophilicity and permeability measurements, on undisclosed terms. PsiThera made it three protein-motion or physics-first chemistry raises in a week: its $25M (Nov 10), with AbbVie Ventures taking a board seat, funds an oral TNFα candidate found with ML plus simulation of transient pockets. Virtual-cell money is spreading to China: on Nov 16 XtalPi-incubated INFevo raised more than RMB 100M, with Aramco's Prosperity7 among new backers, for a multi-omics cell model checked in its own automated lab. And the data argument is now driving where companies get built: Flagship's £100M London origination lab (Nov 16) is explicitly pitched on access to NHS patient data, with UK Biobank and the MHRA among its partners. Model access itself is now venture-scale: Boltz, whose paid models are trained partly on that Excelra data, raised a $110M Series A on Nov 18 led by Bessemer, citing more than 5 million open-model downloads and about 50-fold growth in paid usage in four months, with Pfizer, GSK, Takeda and BMS named as users. At the other end, Tesorai's $5.3M seed (Nov 18), with IQT and Perplexity's fund among backers, bets that re-analysing archived mass-spectrometry proteomics data is a cheaper source of training data than new experiments. And China's virtual-cell race added a second round in a week: YuanShi Tech's Pre-A of nearly RMB 300M (Nov 19), led by Legend Capital, funds data accumulation and an automation platform alongside its models. A third turned up this evening: on Nov 18 IDG Capital led a first round of several hundred million yuan for OneX Intelligence, a Shanghai Jiao Tong spinout with published perturbation, phenotype and pathology models, which will also spend the money on its own wet lab to test predictions. Pharma is also paying for data access on multi-year contracts: on Nov 18 AstraZeneca disclosed a five-year renewal with Tempus AI worth about $200M in fees from 2027, with a $32M yearly minimum, after Tempus delivered a first oncology foundation model in July, and the same day Vertex extended Genomics' human-genetics target platform for four more years at up to more than $220M in milestones plus royalties. The data theme kept going into this week: on Nov 24 Leash Biosciences raised $11M (Innovation Endeavors and Insight Partners) to sell its 44 billion in-house binding measurements as training and test environments for AI scientist agents, and a late-found Nov 18 round showed Shanghai state money and a CSPC-backed fund putting tens of millions of yuan into Xellar's organ-on-chip data platform.

movers.direction: From models to owning life-sciences workflows, and now backing clinical-asset buyers
movers.detail: OpenAI bought Orchestra Bio to put pharma-operations agents into Rosalind and is an investor in Chai, which added Roche on Nov 5 after GSK in October. It also works with Formation Bio (with Sanofi), which just raised a $600M drug-acquisition fund. Alumni are spinning out bio companies: Kevin Weil's Warp, and Miles Wang reportedly raising about $200M. Its startup fund led Biossil's $153M round at a reported $1B, and Biossil has started buying shelved clinical drugs (Theriva's SYN-004 on Nov 2). Another alumna is now signing deals: Fidji Simo's ChronicleBio landed its first drug partner on Nov 12, Prolong, which will fund a trial of PP-007 in ME/CFS patients chosen by ChronicleBio's models. On Nov 20 it published MedChemBench, a 99-problem medicinal-chemistry test on which its newest models score about 84%, while noting the result does not show the models can find new drugs.

movers.direction: From selling Claude to pharma to owning drug programs, now a listed company after an $81.3B IPO
movers.detail: Anthropic's S-1 (Oct 26) frames drug discovery and model-run labs as core uses and names Novo Nordisk, BMS, AbbVie and Sanofi as customers. It disclosed buying Mithril Medicine in July (after Coefficient Bio this spring), is taking its rare-disease antibodies toward candidates in 2027, and its drug R&D head describes two to five active preclinical programs; its Anthology Fund joined Basecamp's $140M. The $70 to $78 range (up to $64.4B plus a $26B private placement) puts it at up to about $1.02T on outstanding shares or about $1.4T fully diluted, and Bloomberg reported orders at about six times the shares on offer by Nov 12; on Nov 18 Anthropic confirmed a price of $83 a share, above the range, selling 980M shares for $81.3B gross, with Nasdaq trading from Nov 19. Per Forbes (Nov 11) it now runs a San Francisco wet lab and intends to hand clinical trials to pharma partners rather than run them itself. Generate Biomedicines' Q3 report (Nov 12) lists a research collaboration with Anthropic on agentic CAR-T design, terms undisclosed. ANT began trading on Nov 19: the first trade was $111.50 and it closed at $97.17, about 17% above the offer price.

movers.direction: Into clinical development through pharma partnerships
movers.detail: Microsoft is testing digital patient twins and synthetic control arms with Boehringer Ingelheim, and Oracle signed a term sheet with AstraZeneca to use hospital data and AI for trial recruitment. Cloud vendors are pitching at the trial stage, while Google's Isomorphic stays in discovery. Specialists are taking the same tools to smaller sponsors: Unlearn's Nov 12 digital-twin analysis for Structure Therapeutics' oral GLP-1.

movers.direction: Converting the AlphaFold lead into $5B of fresh capital, a clinical push and a fourth big-pharma partner
movers.detail: Isomorphic closed a $5B Series C on Nov 17 (Greenoaks and Sequoia co-led; Alphabet kept investing), six months after $2.1B, with the money earmarked for its IsoDDE engine, biologics, partner research and its own clinical development. It also has a data-access roadmap with Abu Dhabi's health department, and with Google DeepMind and Meta put $300M into Biohub's $1.8B open cell-data coalition, reportedly with a one-year head start on the data. On Nov 19 Merck signed it for one oncology small-molecule target using Merck's proprietary data, with an upfront, milestones and royalties (amounts undisclosed) and an option for Isomorphic to co-fund development for higher royalties, its first new partner since the raise.

movers.direction: In the cap tables and now inside lab instruments
movers.detail: NVentures joined Basecamp's $140M Series C, NVIDIA-backed Iambic raised $172.5M in its IPO (with the overallotment), and Danaher is building NVIDIA computing and BioNeMo models into its lab instruments. NVIDIA rarely leads, but it now spans model companies, public drug developers and lab hardware. It is also supplying compute in kind to Biohub's virtual-cell coalition.

movers.direction: Licensing AI platforms for delivery, and holding equity in AI biologics developers
movers.detail: Lilly signed METiS for AI-designed lipid nanoparticles (low double-digit millions upfront, up to $1.1B), adding to its run of AI deals this year. Lilly Ventures is also in Fathom Therapeutics' $55M Series A for physics-plus-AI small-molecule design, which added Kos as an investor on Nov 6. Its older AI-target bets are paying out in steps: on Nov 11 Fauna Bio named a second obesity target from its hibernator-genomics platform under their 2023 pact (up to $494M in milestones), triggering an undisclosed payment.

movers.direction: Spreading AI bets from discovery through preclinical safety to trials, and now locking in five-year access to oncology patient data
movers.detail: AstraZeneca signed insitro for MASH and cardiomyopathy targets, a term sheet with Oracle for AI trial recruitment (starting in Abu Dhabi with M42), a research deal with Tremont AI for AI-read preclinical toxicology, invested in Multiply Labs' $75M round, partners with Pathos on an ER PROTAC and is exploring up to 30 trials in Abu Dhabi by 2030. On Nov 18 it disclosed a renewal of its Tempus AI oncology data and model collaboration for 2027–2031, about $200M in fees with a $32M yearly minimum.

movers.direction: Buying equity and access in AI for neurology and trial planning
movers.detail: BMS led Pathos's $237M Series E, with Alzheimer's as the first focus, and is using Anthropic's Claude to assess early trial plans, with wider work planned for 2027.

movers.direction: Buying an ML-guided oral peptide platform and widening AI antibody design in-house
movers.detail: After more than two years of collaboration and a minority stake, argenx is paying $550M in cash and up to $595M in milestones for Unnatural Products, which will become its peptide discovery hub. It follows the $2.2B Forte Biosciences purchase in July, which was not an AI deal. On Nov 17 it widened its licence to Cradle's AI protein-engineering software to more antibody programs and scientists after a first phase of lead optimisation, on undisclosed terms, so it is adding AI on both its new peptide side and its core antibody side.

movers.direction: Buying AI scientists and shared training data rather than owning AI companies
movers.detail: In one week Pfizer signed Edison Scientific to run its Kosmos agent on internal data across oncology, immunology and internal medicine, and became a founding partner (with GSK and Sanofi) in Parse and Nomic's Cascade immune-perturbation dataset. Neither deal has disclosed terms; both rent capability rather than take equity.

movers.player: Other big & mid-size pharma (Roche, GSK, Astellas, Zealand, Boehringer, UCB, Pierre Fabre, Hansoh, Luoxin, AbbVie, Novo Nordisk, Merck, Vertex)
movers.direction: Licensing AI design platforms across their pipelines rather than building them
movers.detail: Roche signed Chai (Nov 5) to use Chai-3 and its protein-design software across several discovery programs, a month after GSK widened its own Chai deal following lab tests; UCB signed Cradle (Nov 4), joining Bayer, Lundbeck and Hansa as Cradle customers this year, and argenx widened its own Cradle use on Nov 17. Astellas licensed AI Proteins' miniproteins (more than $400M), Zealand hired Generate for obesity proteins ($30M upfront), GSK joined the Cascade immune-data consortium, and Boehringer went to Microsoft for trial twins. Pierre Fabre added XtalPi on Nov 9 for de novo small molecules in oncology, on undisclosed terms. Chinese pharma is on the same path: Hansoh signed AilsynBio on Nov 13 for AI-found oral cyclic peptides, up to RMB317M plus royalties, keeping target choice and IP, and Luoxin followed with a non-binding Insilico cooperation for digestive and metabolic disease (filed Nov 13), with no money attached yet. Venture arms are buying in earlier as well: AbbVie Ventures joined PsiThera's $25M on Nov 10 and took a board seat, backing oral small molecules aimed at immune targets AbbVie now hits with antibodies. Novo Nordisk went downstream on Nov 18, pairing its cardiometabolic trial data with nference's real-world health data and AI for precision-trial design, plus a framework to start new AI-native companies. Merck joined the list on Nov 19, hiring Isomorphic's IsoDDE engine for one oncology small-molecule target on its own data, keeping development and sales in-house. Vertex renewed Genomics' human-genetics target platform on Nov 18 for four more years (up to more than $220M plus royalties), and Astellas added Korea's Bionsight on Nov 19 for an AI-designed autoimmune small molecule.

movers.direction: Merging its US AI platforms into fewer pipeline companies and exporting its company factory to the UK for its patient data
movers.detail: Flagship merged Cellarity, Etiome and Empress (together $374M raised) into Etcelera with no new capital disclosed, spun Cellarity's sickle cell drug into its own company, and is lining up a big-pharma alliance for the combined platform. On Nov 16 it committed an initial £100M (~$132M) to its first origination lab outside Massachusetts, in London, to build AI-native biotechs around NHS data with partners including UK Biobank, the Crick and the MHRA, and hopes to draw £500M or more from others. On Nov 11 it also merged Valo Health and Montai Therapeutics under the Valo name and CEO Brian Alexander, combining causal-biology AI with Montai's chemistry platform around a Phase 1 ulcerative colitis drug; no terms or new money were disclosed.

movers.direction: Concentrating on OpenAI-alumni bio founders
movers.detail: Lightspeed led Warp's $215M launch and is reportedly in talks to lead Miles Wang's ~$200M round.

movers.player: Generalist growth & software VCs (Sequoia, Greenoaks, a16z, Thrive, Bessemer, Insight)
movers.direction: Bringing software-scale cheques to AI drug design, now to open-model platforms as well as drug developers
movers.detail: Greenoaks and Sequoia co-led Isomorphic's $5B Series C on Nov 17, with Andreessen Horowitz joining as a new investor and Thrive, which led the $2.1B Series B in May, returning. These funds usually back software and frontier AI labs, so their entry treats AI drug design as a platform business rather than a pipeline bet. On Nov 18 Bessemer led Boltz's $110M Series A, with a16z, a seed co-lead, investing again; both firms pitch it as a usage-priced software business whose open models already reach top-20 pharma, the same platform logic they apply to coding tools. Insight Partners co-led Leash Biosciences' $11M with Innovation Endeavors on Nov 24, a smaller cheque with the same software logic: Leash sells lab-measured training environments to AI agent builders rather than drugs.

movers.direction: Owning the make-and-test layer end to end
movers.detail: Lux is in Warp (automated chemistry) and Multiply Labs (robotic manufacturing), and earlier this autumn backed Enveda (AI natural-product discovery, now clinical).

movers.direction: Backing data-first and trial-simulation bets
movers.detail: Creandum led Atlas Bio's $10M seed, HV Capital led Rivercell's €22M seed, AVP led WhiteLab's $26M Series B, Asabys led ALLOX's $10.5M seed and PXN Ventures led adsilico's £10M Series A, so European funds are writing larger early cheques for data-first AI biology and virtual-patient simulation. Greek-American Kos Biotechnology Partners took its first AI-discovery stake on Nov 6, joining Fathom's US Series A. Astanor led Biomatter's $18M Series A on Nov 12, with UVC Partners adding to its stake, for AI enzyme design that already has paying customers. On Nov 12 Norrsken VC and Singular co-led Orakl Oncology's $34M Series A for organoid-based trial prediction, with Bpifrance's Patient Autonome Fund among new backers, and Treehouse Delmar put $5M into Switchpoint Bio's blood-biomarker pre-seed on Nov 11.

movers.direction: Positioning for AI-biotech IPOs, late rounds and data partnerships
movers.detail: ARK and Duquesne indicated about 40% of Iambic's IPO, ARK, Janus Henderson and Driehaus took part in Recursion's $200M follow-on, CPP Investments is in Hexagon's Series C, the UK's Sovereign AI fund co-led Potential Sciences' seed and added supercomputer time, the Abu Dhabi Investment Council and Duke's endowment joined Biossil's $153M round, Abu Dhabi is offering its health data to AI drug companies, and the US Energy Department pledged more than $500M over five years to Biohub's open cell-data effort. Aramco's venture arm Prosperity7 joined INFevo's Chinese virtual-cell Pre-A (more than RMB 100M) on Nov 16. MGX, Temasek and the UK Sovereign AI Fund all returned for Isomorphic's $5B Series C (Nov 17). IQT, the US intelligence community's venture arm, backed Tesorai's $5.3M proteomics-data seed on Nov 18. Oman's sovereign fund led MegaRobo's round of nearly $200M (Nov 19) for AI-run robotic labs, the first Gulf-led lab-automation deal in the window.

movers.direction: Funding domestic AI protein design and, now, the human-tissue data that feeds it
movers.detail: China Life Capital led BioGeometry's Series A+, taking its Series A past $100M, with China Development Venture Capital and the Shanghai biomedical fund alongside; the company targets bispecific antibody INDs in 2027. Hong Kong is adding a partnership track: BioMap, hosted with support from the Hong Kong Investment Corporation, announced ten named collaborations on Nov 12 (HKU, Harbour BioMed, Revvity, Temasek Life Sciences Laboratory and others) with no disclosed money. Shanghai's state tech investor led the first of Tourson Intelligence's two Pre-A rounds (several hundred million yuan combined, Nov 9), with MegaRobo joining the second, a second state-led bet on a Chinese AI protein designer in two weeks. Shanghai's state investment manager (Shanghai Guotou Xiandao) joined a drugmaker fund, CSPC Guofang, in Xellar's strategic round of tens of millions of yuan (Nov 18) for organ-on-chip data paired with AI, so state money is now paying for the human-tissue data layer as well as the models.

movers.direction: Funding AI-run drug development asset by asset, not company by company
movers.detail: Unnamed research foundations, endowments, hospitals and philanthropies committed $600M to Formation Bio's first fund, which buys Phase 1–2 drugs into standalone companies. It is the first time this kind of non-venture money has backed an AI drug developer at this scale.

movers.direction: Buying AI-designed molecules from Chinese platforms to seed its own companies
movers.detail: Third Rock committed up to about $2.16B, with an undisclosed platform fee upfront, for Funnel Biosciences to design antibodies against targets it nominates; it is the firm's second such deal with a Chinese AI designer after a peptide pact with Perpetual Medicine that has already produced a development candidate. A venture firm acting like a pharma licensee is new on this map.

movers.player: Chinese venture firms & AI incubators (Qiming, HongShan, Shunwei, Legend, IDG, XtalPi)
movers.direction: Incubating domestic copies of US AI-bio models: virtual cells and agent-run clinical development
movers.detail: On Nov 16 Qiming incubated and solely funded CataX AI's RMB 40M seed for agent-run early clinical development, and XtalPi-incubated INFevo raised more than RMB 100M for a virtual-cell model, with HongShan, Shunwei and Songhe adding to their stakes. They follow Golden Tripod's place in Tourson Intelligence's Pre-A rounds and Zero2IPO's fund in Sanyou's Series C (Nov 9). Rounds are small in dollars and mostly undisclosed in USD, but the bets mirror Formation Bio and the US virtual-cell push. On Nov 19 Legend Capital led YuanShi Tech's Pre-A of nearly RMB 300M for virtual-cell models, with CDH, CMC Capital and a JD.com-linked fund new to the cap table, the second Chinese virtual-cell round in three days and roughly three times INFevo's. IDG Capital joined on Nov 18, leading OneX Intelligence's first round (several hundred million yuan, amount undisclosed) for a university-born virtual-cell and life-science model company, so three Chinese virtual-cell rounds landed in four days, each paired with an in-house lab.

movers.direction: Consolidating sister AI companies into one gene-medicine design platform, paid for in stock
movers.detail: Astromech, co-founded by George Church and Ben Lamm and reportedly valued at $3.8B after raising $60M, agreed on Nov 17 to absorb Form Bio's IP, contracts and team for $230M in stock. The combined company pairs cross-species evolutionary models with vector and construct design for human gene therapies and animal health, and inherits Form Bio's pharma users including Eli Lilly.

predictions.call: At least one more OpenAI or DeepMind alumni bio startup announces a $100M+ launch round
predictions.based_on: Warp's $215M, plus Miles Wang's reported ~$200M round in talks

items.area: Lab-generated training environments for scientific AI agents
items.summary: Salt Lake City's Leash Biosciences, which has made and screened 6.3 million of its own molecules for more than 44 billion binding measurements across nearly 1,000 protein targets, raised $11M co-led by Innovation Endeavors and Insight Partners. It now sells that lab output as Minos, a set of virtual research environments (launched in October) where AI agents run experiments against real measurements.
items.why_invested: Both lead investors framed it as a data bet: Innovation Endeavors called large-scale, high-quality experimental data the main lever left for improving models and liked that the lab and model work sit in one company, and Insight said it backed Leash for measuring ground truth directly. The company's own case is that most drug-discovery data was gathered to find a drug rather than to train a model.
items.whats_next: The money goes into more data production, new training and evaluation environments beyond protein–small-molecule binding, and partnerships with AI developers and pharma; none are named yet. Leash says it will soon publish results showing its environments improve model performance, which is the claim to check, along with a first named AI-lab or pharma customer.
items.why_it_matters: A first round priced on selling experiments to AI agents rather than drugs to pharma, the same data-shortage thesis as Tesorai and the Cascade consortium, now aimed at the agent builders.

items.summary: Merck (MSD outside the US and Canada) signed Isomorphic Labs to design small-molecule candidates against one undisclosed oncology target. Isomorphic runs predictions and proposes molecules with its IsoDDE engine on proprietary data Merck supplies; Merck takes candidates through preclinical and clinical development, manufacturing and sales.
items.why_invested: Merck's stated case is that AI molecular design works only when the computational and wet-lab teams work closely together, and that pairing its own internal data and chemistry know-how with Isomorphic's models and compute should yield better candidates faster. Isomorphic presents it as a hard program on which to prove IsoDDE.
items.whats_next: Merck pays an upfront and Isomorphic can earn research, development, regulatory and sales milestones plus tiered royalties; no amounts or timelines were disclosed. Isomorphic can choose to co-fund development for higher royalties, so watch whether it exercises that option, which would be its first step into sharing clinical costs on a partnered drug, whether the target is named, and whether terms surface in Alphabet or Merck filings.
items.why_it_matters: Two days after closing $5B, Isomorphic added a fourth big-pharma partner after Lilly, Novartis and J&J, and the co-fund option shows AI designers starting to buy into the downstream economics instead of taking only fees and milestones.

items.summary: Boltz, the MIT spinout behind the open Boltz-1 and Boltz-2 structure and affinity models and the BoltzGen designer, raised a $110M Series A led by Bessemer, with seed co-lead a16z investing again. It now sells paid small-molecule and protein design models (BoltzMol-1, BoltzProt-1), an API that plugs into coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and custom models trained on a customer's own data, with Pfizer, GSK, Takeda and BMS named as users.
items.why_invested: Bessemer's stated case is that open models scientists already trusted (more than 5 million downloads) give Boltz a head start as preclinical screening and design move from the bench to the computer, and that returns grow as the models improve. a16z points to customer usage of its paid models rising about 50-fold in roughly four months after the BoltzMol-1 and BoltzProt-1 launches, and to a usage-priced model where customers keep what they design.
items.whats_next: Use of funds was not disclosed. Watch for a named pharma deal larger than a software licence, the first custom models trained on partner data, whether the 50-fold usage growth turns into disclosed revenue, what it does with the measured property data it now licenses from Excelra (Nov 11), and whether open releases keep pace with the paid products.
items.why_it_matters: Investors are now paying growth-style prices for an open-model company that sells usage rather than drugs, a bet that model access, not pipelines, can be a big business in AI biology.

items.summary: San Diego's Tesorai raised a $5.3M seed (about $8M in total) for AI that re-analyses raw mass-spectrometry proteomics data, new and archived, so scientists and models can query it. It sells a search engine for raw spectra, a curated catalogue of public proteomics studies and a chat interface, and works with MD Anderson, NYU and the Michael J. Fox Foundation.
items.why_invested: The company's case is that AI drug discovery is short of usable biological data and that much of what already exists in past experiments is under-analysed. Likely: Perplexity's fund sees a search-and-answer layer for scientific data, and IQT, the US intelligence community's venture arm, sees value in mining existing biological datasets.
items.whats_next: It plans to sign more biopharma and tools-industry partners, add more public studies to its catalogue and extend beyond proteins to other molecular data. Watch for a named pharma contract and for any published benchmark against standard proteomics search tools.
items.why_it_matters: A small bet on reusing existing experiments, the cheap end of the same data shortage that big consortia like Biohub and Cascade are paying to fix with new data.

Planned work covers clinical pharmacology, combination therapies and precision trials that track whole-body health alongside weight loss, plus a framework for starting new AI-native companies in cardiometabolic health and ageing. No financial terms were given.
items.why_invested: Novo's stated aim is to use AI and data to understand cardiometabolic disease more deeply and shape future treatments. Likely: with obesity drugs moving into combinations and long-term use, Novo wants real-world outcome data beyond its own trials, and the venture framework gives it first look at companies built on that data.
items.whats_next: Watch for the first published analyses, whether precision-trial designs show up in Novo's obesity or combination programs, and whether the venture framework produces a named company or funding commitment.
items.why_it_matters: A top obesity drug maker is treating real-world health data and AI as a development tool and a company-creation channel, pushing AI further downstream from discovery into trial design.

items.summary: Shanghai's OneX Intelligence, a Shanghai Jiao Tong University AI-school spinout led by CEO and chief scientist Xie Weidi, closed its first round, reported as several hundred million yuan, led by IDG Capital. items.area: Gene therapy design AI / evolutionary genomics models
items.summary: Astromech, the Dallas AI company co-founded by George Church and Ben Lamm that models how biological sequences change across species, is taking over Form Bio's IP, selected contracts, assets and team in an all-stock deal valued at $230M. Form Bio, launched inside Colossal Biosciences in 2022 with over $40M raised, builds AI tools for designing gene-therapy constructs and vectors and checking genome quality; both companies come out of Colossal.
items.why_invested: The companies say joining Astromech's evolutionary models to Form Bio's construct-design tools lets researchers go straight from spotting evolutionary patterns to designing and testing genetic constructs, catching quality problems such as unwanted genome fragments at the design stage rather than in purification. They point to a Duchenne program with Cure Rare Disease where promoter redesign lifted full-genome content from 13% to 59% in under 30 days. Likely also: Astromech, which raised $60M by August at a reported $3.8B valuation, is using its richly priced stock to buy a team and paying customers rather than building them.
items.whats_next: Andrew Busey, Form Bio's co-founder and CEO, becomes Astromech's chief AI officer and head of technology, taking the headcount to about 65. No closing conditions or timeline were given. Watch whether Form Bio's gene-medicine customers (Eli Lilly, Taysha, Solid Biosciences, Coave, Stanford) stay on and widen their contracts, whether the Duchenne construct reaches IND-enabling work, and whether Astromech raises again or launches its own human or animal-health programs.
items.why_it_matters: AI design is reaching genetic medicines, not just small molecules and antibodies, and well-valued AI-bio companies are starting to use their stock as acquisition currency to consolidate smaller tool makers.

items.why_invested: Likely: the stake gives Quanome a life-sciences leg for its quantum strategy; the two plan a collaboration on AI drug discovery after closing. Quantum algorithms are so far being explored only on classical simulators.
items.whats_next: Closing is subject to customary conditions and the shares are unregistered. QAI is pre-commercial, with candidates still needing lab validation.
items.why_it_matters: Low signal on its own: a stock-for-stock valuation between two small companies, included mostly as a marker of how far the AI-drug label now stretches.

items.area: Causal virtual cell plus patient genomics
items.summary: Paris-based DeepLife, whose TwinCell causal cell model is built on single-cell multi-omics data, signed a co-development deal with KOSDAQ-listed Korean genomics company 3billion to find small molecules against genetic modifiers, the genes that change how severely a disease shows up in people carrying the same mutation. No financial terms were disclosed.
items.why_invested: Stated: each side holds half of the path. DeepLife's model nominates causal targets, 3billion checks them against the genomes from its rare-disease testing business, which the release puts at more than 110,000 people, and designs compounds with its own AI chemistry tools. Modifier targets offer a way in when the disease gene itself resists drugging.
items.whats_next: The partners plan to carry programs through preclinical and IND-enabling work and then license them to larger pharma. No indications, timelines or milestones were named. Watch for a first disclosed target and whether a pharma partner joins.
items.why_it_matters: Two mid-size AI companies are pooling a virtual-cell model with a proprietary patient-genome cohort to own the assets themselves, a sign that data holders outside big pharma would rather take a stake in drugs than sell access.

Greek-American fund Kos Biotechnology Partners said on Nov 6 it has joined Fathom's Sutter Hill-led Series A, now put at $55M; Kos's own cheque was not disclosed.
items.why_invested: Kos says it is betting that simulation-plus-AI raises discovery productivity and opens targets that static-structure methods cannot reach; earlier backers include Lilly Ventures, which ties a large pharma to the approach.
items.whats_next: Fathom hired Bret Williams (ex-Magnet Biomedicine, Relay, Sanofi) as CSO on Oct 29 to turn Microcosmos designs into named programs, so watch for its first disclosed targets, a first pharma partnership, and a Series B once programs reach candidate stage.
items.why_it_matters: A second physics-first chemistry bet in two days (after Potential Sciences) suggests investors now see simulated molecular dynamics, not just more lab data, as a way to beat static structure models on hard targets.

items.summary: Funnel Biosciences, a Beijing AI antibody designer co-founded in February 2026 by former MSD researcher Jintan Liu and computational biophysicist Mingchen Chen, will design biologics against several targets picked by Boston venture firm Third Rock. Funnel gets an undisclosed platform-access fee and up to about $2.16B in total if the programs advance; Endpoints and pharmaphorum reported it on Nov 9 and 10.
items.why_invested: Stated by Funnel: its epitope-first generative design, refined with physics-based energy scoring, is meant to crack hard targets such as multi-pass membrane proteins where animal immunisation and phage display struggle, and Third Rock brings translation and company-building. Likely: Third Rock wants de novo antibodies for hard targets to seed its own new companies, sourced from a fast, lower-cost Chinese design shop rather than built in-house.
items.whats_next: No targets, rights split or timelines were disclosed. Watch for the first development candidate (Third Rock's earlier peptide pact with Shanghai's Perpetual Medicine produced one in under 18 months), a Third Rock company launched around a Funnel antibody, Funnel's own first financing, and any US scrutiny of China-sourced biologics.
items.why_it_matters: A US venture firm, not a pharma, is now signing pharma-style biobucks deals with Chinese AI designers to stock its company-creation pipeline, so China's AI biologics shops have a second kind of Western buyer.

items.summary: Venomics AI, a Bengaluru spinout of the Indian Institute of Science, sequences animal-venom molecules into a dataset it calls the Venom Atlas, ranks candidates with AI and checks them in its own lab screens. It closed a $2.7M pre-seed, its first institutional round, co-led by Speciale Invest and South Park Commons.
items.why_invested: Likely: the backers are buying a proprietary dataset in a largely untapped chemical space, where a closed loop of AI ranking and wet-lab testing can turn venom peptides into drug leads that public data cannot reach.
items.whats_next: The money goes to growing the Venom Atlas, building out AI and lab screening, hiring across venom biology and computation, and validating its first leads. Watch for a named lead program or a first pharma or biodefense partner.
items.why_it_matters: Even at pre-seed, investors back the data-first model: a small team wins funding by owning an unusual dataset plus the lab to generate more of it, the same logic behind ALLOX, Rivercell and the larger cell-data coalitions.

items.why_invested: Likely: Roche wants frontier protein-design models without building them itself, while keeping wet-lab work and program ownership in house; Chai's record of wet-lab validation at GSK and other partners lowers the risk of a platform-wide rollout.
items.whats_next: Chai's tools go into multiple Roche programs. Watch for disclosed terms, whether Genentech is included, the first Roche program credited to Chai designs, and a new Chai raise on the back of its partner list.
items.why_it_matters: Chai now has seven big-pharma and biotech partners in about ten months (Lilly, Pfizer, Novartis, argenx, BMS, GSK and now Roche), so licensing a generative design model is becoming standard procurement at top pharma rather than an experiment.

items.summary: Potential Sciences, a UK startup founded a year ago by former Graphcore executive Hatem Helal, came out of stealth with an eight-figure seed round co-led by Twin Path Ventures and the government's Sovereign AI fund. It rebuilds quantum-chemistry simulation for GPUs so its drug-design models can train on physics-generated data rather than past lab experiments.
items.why_invested: Sovereign AI says it wants the company to become a frontier lab for chemistry and is adding compute on the Isambard-AI supercomputer; the company's pitch is that AI chemistry models are short of good data and that physics-based calculation could cut the cost of that data by about 100x.
items.whats_next: Use of funds was not detailed. Watch for its first model release or benchmarks, a first pharma or materials partner, and how much Isambard-AI compute it is allotted.
items.why_it_matters: A third answer to biology's data shortage is getting funded: alongside open coalitions (Biohub) and pharma-shared datasets (Cascade), investors are now backing startups that generate training data by simulation, with the UK state backing it directly.

It paid $750K cash, up to $1.25M on delivery milestones and $2.5M in locked-up stock, and took the code, model weights and data rights.
items.why_invested: iSpecimen says it wants to move from supplying samples to helping researchers choose protein targets, pairing its specimen network with the acquired models and adding software revenue.
items.whats_next: Two $625K payments fall due once the products pass acceptance tests; watch whether iSpecimen launches a paid target-discovery product and whether any pharma customer signs up.
items.why_it_matters: Small, but the pattern is the same as in larger deals: companies that hold human biological samples are trying to sell AI insight on top of them rather than just the samples.

items.summary: Amsterdam-based Cradle, which sells an AI protein-engineering platform that learns from each round of lab results, signed a strategic collaboration with Belgian drugmaker UCB. UCB will run Cradle's software on selected antibody and biologics discovery projects, from first hits through lead optimization to preclinical readiness; no financial terms, duration or programs were disclosed.
items.why_invested: UCB's research chief frames AI as a support tool for its scientists, with the payoff coming from pairing model predictions with wet-lab testing to reach better molecules faster. Likely also: UCB is assembling a set of outside AI tools around its in-house digital antibody program (it already licenses XtalPi's Ailux structure software and runs the DARC antibody-AI effort with the University of Southampton) rather than betting on one vendor.
items.whats_next: Watch for which UCB programs (immunology or CNS) move onto the platform, whether the deal is later widened across the biologics pipeline, as Cradle's CEO suggested, and whether any financial terms or a first candidate surface. For Cradle, this is a fourth pharma software deal in 2026 after Bayer (January), Lundbeck (June) and Hansa (October); a new funding round would be the next signal.
items.why_it_matters: Antibody-design AI is turning into licensed software that mid-size pharma rolls out program by program, a recurring-seat model that sits apart from the milestone-heavy drug-discovery deals.

items.summary: Toronto-based Biossil, an AI-native company that hunts for shelved drug candidates and develops them itself, agreed to buy Theriva Biologics' antibiotic-degrading enzyme portfolio, led by SYN-004 (ribaxamase), plus SYN-007 and SYN-006-related assets. Theriva gets $350K at closing, up to $3M in regulatory and $88M in sales milestones, and capped low single-digit royalties; Biossil takes on all further costs.
items.why_invested: Likely: the asset fits Biossil's model of buying molecules that stalled for business reasons rather than failed on biology, here a Phase 1b/2a enzyme meant to protect the gut microbiome of stem-cell transplant patients. Theriva says the sale keeps the program alive while it focuses on its oncolytic virus VCN-01. The near-zero upfront shows the seller had little leverage.
items.whats_next: Biossil plans to restart the paused Washington University Phase 1b/2a trial in allogeneic transplant patients (two of three cohorts done, with a third planned on IV cefepime, up to 36 evaluable patients). Watch for the trial reopening, and for more cheap buys of shelved assets with the $153M it raised in September.
items.why_it_matters: OpenAI-backed capital is now flowing through AI-native developers into the clinic by buying shelved assets for almost nothing upfront, the same play Formation Bio is funding with $600M.

It combines more than 30 prediction models, a foundation model trained on about 150 million cells and Flagship's in-house AI unit; no new funding was announced.

items.summary: Barcelona's ALLOX, a spinout of the Centre for Genomic Regulation, maps allosteric pockets by testing huge numbers of protein mutants at once and is building AI models on that data to find druggable sites on hard targets. items.why_invested: Likely: Asabys, which also led the pre-seed, is backing a proprietary biophysical dataset that few others have, aimed at protein-protein interactions and transcription factors that standard design tools struggle with.
items.whats_next: Building its AI hotspot models, growing the in-house chemistry team, moving several programs toward small-molecule candidates and signing pharma research partnerships.
items.why_it_matters: Another European seed built on generating its own experimental data first, the same bet as Rivercell and Atlas Bio.

items.summary: Brooklyn-founded Opentrons sells open, low-cost liquid-handling robots (Flex and OT-2) that AI systems can drive to design, run and adjust experiments in a loop. It has more than 11,000 robots in over 80 countries and raised a $40M Series E led by healthcare investor Avego.
items.why_invested: Avego's stated view is that every AI-generated hypothesis still has to be tested at a real bench, so the robots that run those tests become a standard layer for autonomous science, and Opentrons already sits in most top-20 pharma labs. Likely also: the installed base gives a cheap route to selling AI software and data tools on top of hardware already in place.
items.whats_next: Spend on AI-driven experiment execution, faster protocol writing through software and AI, tighter links to other lab instruments, and new regions. Watch for agent or model integrations (e.g. with frontier AI labs) and whether the smaller round, well below its $200M SoftBank-led Series C in 2021, signals a flat or lower valuation.
items.why_it_matters: Lab-robot makers are now pitching themselves as the execution layer for AI scientists, the same bet behind Warp, Multiply Labs and Danaher's NVIDIA tie-up, but from the low-cost, high-volume end of the market.

items.why_invested: Edison's pitch is that Kosmos learns from Pfizer's own record of what has worked and failed in human biology and carries lessons between programs, giving Pfizer a compounding in-house advantage rather than a one-off tool. Likely also: Pfizer wants a pipeline-wide agent deal of its own after rivals signed with Anthropic, OpenAI and others.
items.whats_next: Kosmos will build combined world models from public data and Pfizer's internal data, and Edison is embedding its own scientists and engineers in Pfizer teams. Watch for disclosed terms, a named program or decision credited to Kosmos, more pharma signings after Incyte (May) and Pfizer, and whether Edison raises a larger round on the back of it.
items.why_it_matters: Big pharma is now signing pipeline-wide AI-scientist deals with startups as well as frontier labs, and the value being sold is training on the pharma's private failure data, not the model alone.

items.whats_next: Watch for the first data release and timeline, more pharma or AI-lab partners joining, and whether any partner reports a target or model trained on it. Also watch whether access terms stay closed or loosen given Biohub's open data push.
items.why_it_matters: Pharma is now paying, as a group, for the perturbation data that virtual-cell models need, a closed, licensed counterpart to the big tech-funded open Biohub effort.

items.summary: Formation Bio, the New York AI-native drug developer that works with Sanofi and OpenAI, closed $600M in commitments for its first fund, the Drug Development Accelerator Fund. The fund will only finance Phase 1 and 2 drugs Formation buys or in-licenses, each held in its own company. No LPs were named.
items.why_invested: Stated: LPs get exposure to single drug programs without funding a whole biotech, and Formation gets cheaper capital, more programs and ways to cash out without selling the parent. Its bet is that the bottleneck is pushing stalled clinical drugs through trials, not finding molecules. Likely: mission-driven LPs (foundations, hospitals) like the focus on neglected diseases with little active development.
items.whats_next: Acquire or license 10 to 15 clinical-stage programs over 3 to 5 years, aiming for major clinical results 2 to 4 years after each deal, then partner them with pharma. Watch for the first fund-backed in-licensing deals, the sellers (pharma reprioritizations, distressed biotechs), and whether its AI actually shortens trials.
items.why_it_matters: A first for the field: an AI drug developer raising a fund-style vehicle from non-venture LPs to buy clinical assets one by one. It is not counted as a venture round, but it moves serious money toward AI-run development rather than discovery.

items.summary: Tremont AI, a Boston spinout from the Mahmood Lab at Mass General Brigham that builds foundation models and agents for reading preclinical toxicology slides, signed a research collaboration with AstraZeneca to build and test AI for faster safety screening in animal studies. No financial terms were disclosed; trade coverage appeared Oct 28–30.
items.why_invested: Tremont's stated case is that pathologists still score huge numbers of tissue images by semi-quantitative judgment that varies between experts, and that toxicology-specific models can make those reads measurable, repeatable and quicker to triage, especially rare findings that general-purpose models miss. Likely for AstraZeneca: a cheap way to speed up the safety step that sits between AI-designed molecules and the clinic, building on its earlier pathology-AI moves such as the Modella acquisition.
items.whats_next: The two will refine and benchmark Tremont's models on real safety-assessment work; no timeline or milestones were given. Watch for published validation results, a move from research collaboration to paid deployment, other pharma or CRO signings, and a disclosed seed round for Tremont, which only came out of stealth in late September.
items.why_it_matters: As AI speeds up design, pharma is starting to pay for AI further down the preclinical chain, where safety reads are a slow manual step.

The founders come from Google language-model research and self-driving cars, which also appealed to tech-first investors.
items.whats_next: Hiring across science and sales, platform work, and signing enterprise customers. The company says first simulated-trial results are due roughly six weeks after the announcement (around early December); watch for a named pharma customer and any prospective validation against a real trial readout.

items.summary: Anthropic disclosed that in July it bought Mithril Medicine, a one-person, Atlas-backed startup whose founder used Claude to coordinate 11 outside labs and take a bispecific antibody for LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy from idea to mouse data in under 18 months. Terms were not disclosed; Anthropic also published early results from Claude work with BMS, Enveda, Generate, BigHat, Divergence Labs and The Column Group.
items.why_invested: Anthropic frames it as a shift from supplying AI tools to pharma toward developing its own medicines, starting with rare childhood diseases, under a model it calls one scientist running several programs with AI doing the coordination. Likely: owning programs gives it hard case studies of what Claude can and cannot do across the whole pipeline, which helps sell to pharma.

The mouse data is preliminary. BMS plans to widen its Claude trial-planning work in 2027.

items.area: Virtual patients for in-silico device trials
items.summary: adsilico, a 2024 University of Leeds spinout, uses generative AI on anonymised scans to build virtual hearts and vessels, then runs physics simulations to test implants across varied virtual populations before and alongside clinical trials. It raised a £10M Series A, taking its total to £13.5M.
items.why_invested: Likely: device trials enrol only a few hundred patients and struggle to cover every body type, so investors are backing software that lets makers spot risky patient groups and choose sizes before costly studies. PXN led, with existing backers Northern Gritstone and Parkwalk following on.
items.whats_next: Building out heart models, expanding into neurovascular devices such as aneurysm flow diverters, and growing from 14 to about 34 staff. Watch for named device-maker customers and whether regulators accept its simulations as supporting evidence.
items.why_it_matters: Virtual-patient modelling is spreading from drug trials into medical devices, adding to the case that simulated cohorts will become a standard part of trial evidence.

items.summary: Boehringer Ingelheim and Microsoft agreed a strategic collaboration to test whether AI-built digital patient twins can model disease progression, simulate trials and support synthetic or hybrid control arms. Work starts in lung health; no financial terms were given.
items.why_invested: Boehringer says the aim is fewer patients on placebo, faster evidence and better-designed trials, while keeping regulatory and safety standards intact. Likely: Microsoft gains a flagship pharma use case for its cloud and AI stack, building on Boehringer's large Copilot rollout.
items.whats_next: A feasibility phase of modelling and prototyping in lung disease, then possible expansion to other therapy areas, animal health and infrastructure work. No timeline was disclosed; watch for a first hybrid control arm and any regulator engagement.
items.why_it_matters: Big pharma and big tech are taking AI past discovery and into the design of the trials themselves, where most of the money is spent.

items.summary: Xaira unveiled X-Automate: lab workcells, a low-cost vision-guided robotic arm (X-Bot), and an AI agent (X-Scientist) that runs the experiments. In a week-long test, instrument use went from an estimated 54% on a 9-to-5 human schedule to 97%.

items.why_invested: Not a deal. Xaira is spending its existing funding on in-house, low-cost robotics instead of buying expensive lab automation.
items.whats_next: A planned self-driving lab with about 100 robot arms and a mobile robot platform (Eve). Long-term reliability is still unproven.

items.summary: Pathos uses its Foundry platform, which draws on a very large oncology data set, to pick cancer drug candidates, identify the patients most likely to respond, and design biomarker-driven trials. The new money funds four drug programs, led by the ADC JSKN016.
items.why_it_matters: A big pharma leading a late-stage round at a $3B valuation signals confidence in AI-first clinical development, not just discovery.
items.why_invested: BMS gets equity plus a working partnership: its first joint focus is Alzheimer's, so the money buys BMS a direct line into Pathos's agent-driven candidate scoring as Pathos moves from oncology into neurology. The round came in below the reported $300M target, but the valuation still nearly doubled from $1.6B in May 2025.
items.whats_next: Neurology expansion built on new datasets from Tempus AI; the BMS Alzheimer's program; pushing the JSKN016 ADC and the AstraZeneca ER PROTAC program forward. Watch for first neurology candidates and any BMS opt-in rights.

items.summary: Hexagon Bio mines microbial genomes with a computational discovery platform to find new cell-killing small molecules. It closed a $62M Series C led by The Column Group to take its first antibody-drug conjugate, HEX-360, into the clinic.
items.why_invested: Stated: HEX-360 pairs a HER2 antibody with a payload that blocks protein production, which the company argues can get around resistance to today's topoisomerase and tubulin payloads; preclinical data at AACR 2026 matched or beat an Enhertu-like comparator. Likely: investors are buying a novel-payload ADC story at a time when ADCs are pharma's hottest licensing category.
items.whats_next: HEX-360 is in IND-enabling studies, with a Phase 1 start guided for the first half of 2027. The money also funds new single and dual payloads. Watch for the IND filing and any pharma ADC partnership.
items.why_it_matters: Computational discovery platforms are increasingly being funded on the strength of one clinical-ready asset, not on the platform itself.

items.summary: Isomorphic Labs and Abu Dhabi's Department of Health will draw up a 24-month roadmap for AI-enabled preclinical research inside the emirate's secure research data environment.
items.why_it_matters: Gulf states are trading access to population health data for a role in AI drug discovery. That data access is becoming a competitive advantage in its own right.
items.why_invested: Abu Dhabi is trading access to its health data and research environment for a role in AI drug discovery. Isomorphic gets data from populations that are underrepresented in drug research.
items.whats_next: A 24-month preclinical research roadmap. In a parallel agreement, AstraZeneca explores up to 30 trials in Abu Dhabi by 2030, with the first six by end of 2026.

items.summary: Founded by Kevin Weil, OpenAI's former science lead. Human chemists wearing cameras and sensor gloves train robots that synthesize and test compounds around the clock. The company also wants to bring outsourced molecule synthesis back onshore.
items.why_it_matters: One of the largest debut rounds for a wet-lab automation company. It targets the step where most AI drug-discovery pipelines slow down: making and testing the molecules.
items.why_invested: Two stated reasons. First, drugmakers depend on Chinese contract labs such as WuXi AppTec for molecule optimization, which looks riskier amid US–China tension and data-security worries. Second, frontier AI hasn't transformed experiment-driven chemistry the way it has software, because models need real lab data. Warp produces that data, using robots trained on chemists' movements, in the US. Angels include OpenAI CFO Sarah Friar, Brian Armstrong and Reid Hoffman.
items.whats_next: Build a fully automated US lab for drug optimization (not discovery). The team of about 20 has already bought robot arms and AI chips. No timeline was given. Watch for a first pharma customer and the lab's opening.

items.summary: AstraZeneca and Oracle signed a non-binding term sheet to use Oracle's cloud, AI tools and de-identified hospital data to find trial patients sooner, spot disease earlier and monitor drug safety. The first project is an uncontrolled-hypertension program in Abu Dhabi with UAE health company M42.
items.why_invested: The stated goal is to cut the slow patient enrollment that makes trials long and costly, pairing Oracle's data and AI with AstraZeneca's trial and regulatory know-how. Likely: Oracle gets a top pharma anchor for its health-data business, and AstraZeneca extends its Abu Dhabi trial push.
items.whats_next: Terms still have to be finalised. More projects are planned in the US, Middle East and Europe across cancer, cardiorenal, respiratory, immunology and rare disease, each after legal, privacy and ethics review.
items.why_it_matters: A second big pharma–big tech trial-AI tie-up in a week (after Boehringer–Microsoft) shows the spending moving to recruitment and trial execution.

items.summary: Hong Kong's METiS, which uses its AiLNP platform to generate and optimise ionizable lipids for lipid nanoparticles, signed a delivery collaboration with Eli Lilly. METiS gets an upfront in the low double-digit millions, up to $1.1B in milestones and single-digit tiered royalties.
items.why_invested: Lilly wants nanoparticles that reach specific tissues and perform better, and METiS argues delivery often decides whether a drug works. Likely: Lilly is buying optionality on delivery for its growing nucleic-acid and genetic-medicine pipeline without building lipid design in-house.
items.whats_next: Lipid discovery and optimisation for undisclosed Lilly programs; no diseases or timelines named. Watch for the first named indication and whether METiS adds more Western pharma partners after Hengrui and Boulevard Bio.
items.why_it_matters: AI deal flow is spreading from designing molecules to designing how they get delivered, and pharma will source that from China-based platforms despite US policy pressure.

items.summary: San Francisco's Capable is building its own lab that turns AI-generated drug designs into experimental data quickly enough for each result to steer the next design, starting with peptides aimed at reducing how much sleep people need. Its $38M seed, disclosed in a mid-October company update and reported by Dealroom on Oct 20, brings total funding to about $50M and pays for a lab that grew from 2,000 to 22,500 sq ft in Mission Bay.
items.why_invested: Likely: backers are paying for the design-to-data loop rather than a model, betting that a company owning chemistry, biology, hardware and ML under one roof can iterate faster than ones that outsource testing; the angel list (Karpathy, Simo) signals frontier-AI people backing a wet-lab bottleneck thesis. No lead or valuation was disclosed.
items.whats_next: The first program, in sleep, is entering preclinical safety testing by the company's own account; watch for a named candidate, safety data, more programs on the same platform, and whether the scaled lab is offered to outside partners.
items.why_it_matters: Another sign that early money is going to companies that own the lab loop end to end, not just the design model, even at seed stage.

items.summary: NVIDIA-backed Iambic, which designs small-molecule cancer drugs with its own AI platform, priced its Nasdaq IPO at $16, the middle of its range. With the underwriters' option fully exercised it sold about 10.8M shares for $172.5M gross (about $156M net).
items.why_invested: Likely: public investors get a clinical-stage AI drug developer with a Phase 1 asset (IAM1363, a brain-penetrant HER2 inhibitor) and a long list of pharma partners. Existing holders ARK and Duquesne signalled they would take about 40% of the deal, which de-risked the book.
items.whats_next: About $75M goes to mid-stage work on IAM1363, about $15M each to IAM217 (KIF18A) and IAM-C1 (CDK2/4), and about $20M to the AI platform. Its first public quarterly report (Nov 16) put pro forma cash at about $455M including AbbVie's roughly $47M upfront; watch IAM217 preclinical data at EORTC-NCI-AACR (Nov 18–20), the IAM-C1 IND this quarter, and a registrational HER2+ breast cancer study for IAM1363 planned for 2027.
items.why_it_matters: The IPO window is open again for AI-native drugmakers with clinical assets, giving late-stage private rounds a public exit to price against.

items.summary: Recursion sold about 61.5M shares at $3.25 to raise roughly $200M, on the same day Sanofi picked the first development candidate from their AI small-molecule collaboration, an oral drug for inflammatory disease that triggers a $10M milestone. The shares jumped more than 16% on the Sanofi news.
items.why_invested: Likely: specialist holders such as Janus Henderson, ARK and Driehaus bought in on the first pharma-picked candidate from the platform, which adds validation and lifts total Sanofi payments to $144M.
items.whats_next: Recursion's Q3 report (Nov 2) put cash at about $562M at quarter end, roughly $749M counting the October offering, with runway into 2029. On the call, management said the Sanofi-optioned molecule is an oral dual-target inflammation drug that its AI platform helped design; Sanofi now leads and funds it, Phase 1 is planned for 2027, and each such program carries up to $343M in milestones plus royalties. Genentech has also optioned a first neuroscience target from Recursion's biological maps, and total partner cash received now tops $535M. Clinically, REC-4881 cut polyp burden in 13 of 15 FAP patients at 12 weeks (median 47%), and the Nov 3 investor webinar walked through that data; a registrational study is targeted for the second half of 2027 if the FDA agrees on design, and analysts were told it will likely need to show hard outcomes. Watch more partner milestones in 2027 and how the stock holds after the data.
items.why_it_matters: First-generation AI biotechs can still raise from public markets, but at a discount and only when a pharma partner backs a molecule.

items.summary: Danaher, which owns Beckman Coulter, Leica, Cytiva and other lab-instrument businesses, agreed to build NVIDIA computing and AI into its instruments: DGX Spark at the edge, RAPIDS analytics and BioNeMo models, with Cosmos and Omniverse digital twins being explored. A small set of priority instruments comes first. No financial terms were given.
items.why_invested: Both sides say the aim is a closed loop in which experiment results train models and models choose the next experiments, which shortens the step from prediction to proof. For NVIDIA it puts its stack inside the installed base of lab hardware. Danaher keeps customers free to use other models, which suggests it wants AI as an instrument feature rather than a lock-in.
items.whats_next: Pilot results on the first instruments, then a decision on rolling out across the portfolio. Watch for named pharma pilot sites and for links to Danaher's own autonomous antibody lab.
items.why_it_matters: The incumbent instrument makers now want the 'AI lab' business that startups such as Lila, Warp and Multiply are raising for, and NVIDIA is supplying both sides.
